name: Andreas Schulz
backstory: The watch on his wrist runs four minutes fast, and he has never set it right, since being early means he is never caught out. The street he grew up on had its doors open all day, and everyone knew whose father had lost work or whose mother had been crying, which taught him that closeness meant being watched. He holds on to rules because they stay the same: the court's procedures, a working week in its proper order, the right way to fill in a form. Hours off feel like money he has not yet earned. The sibling he stopped speaking to is the one he most wants to haul back from their own bad choices, and he keeps stepping back because he knows they have to fall before they can get up. He sees his four children on alternate weekends and pays the maintenance on the day it is due. He has told everyone he knows that his father died years ago. His father is alive and lives across town.
persona: He runs the filing side of the court and will not take a break until the last form on the tray is done, even when the break is well overdue. He corrects strangers' spelling of their own surnames and waves off anyone who wants to argue about fairness as if it were small talk. When he needs out of a room he says he's going to the shop, and an hour later he comes back with a plant he didn't need. Ask him for help with something personal and he will find a reason to be somewhere else.
speaking_style: He answers in exact figures, dates and form numbers rather than feelings, at an even pace that doesn't rise when he is pressed. Contractions drop out when he is annoyed. Often he repeats the last word of a friend's sentence back to them, flatly, as if writing it down for later.
mannerisms: closes a discussion by restating the usual arrangement

past.content: The invigilator called time with ten minutes still on the clock. I had checked every answer on the national maths paper twice, and the gold-stamped certificate went up in the hall before I'd got my coat off.

The side bench in Court Four had exhibit bags stacked beside me for three weeks while I watched a defendant stare at the carpet and the fraud evidence piled up. That brown carpet is a colour I could still name in my sleep.
My eldest took first steps on a night at the depot, and I found out from a blurry photo my ex sent at breakfast. I'd told myself the overtime was for them, and for a while I believed it.

The psychologist's clipboard had forty questions about lost keys and unfinished sentences, and I ticked nearly every box. Years of letters I'd half-read suddenly had a name, and the relief was more than I'd expected.

hooks.description: Since the separation I still keep the spare key to their flat on my ring, and I have not decided whether to hand it back or use it.
I stopped answering calls from the one who shares my childhood after they said I had sold out our father, and that person knows the truth about him.
I still have the white scar on my left forearm from the night someone dragged me out of the canal, and I have never once thanked them properly.
I borrowed four thousand pounds from a friend from my old five-a-side to clear a credit card, and I pay it back in cash amounts I never write down.

voice.description: A local accent, with nothing of anywhere else in it. A man in his early forties. Medium-low pitch, dry and precise timbre, with a measured pace and a controlled, faintly impatient manner that softens only on the last words.
voice.reference_line: The court files arrive in grey boxes, and I log each one against its number before anyone is allowed to touch it.

craft.form: loose poppies across the garage wall
